0.0.n: 歳 counts years of age and combines with の here to describe the children.

0.1.n: Links the age to 男女, making it describe how old the children are.

0.2.n: Usually means males and females; the age makes it refer to children here.

0.3.n: Marks the three-year-olds as the group being discussed.

0.4.n: The first part of 髪置, the ceremony name marking when children began growing their hair out.

0.5.n: Part of the ceremony name 髪置, not a separate verb here.

1.0.n: 歳 counts years of age; の connects this age to 男子.

1.1.n: Links the age to 男子, describing the boys as five years old.

1.2.n: Refers specifically to male children in this age-based ceremony description.

1.3.n: Introduces the five-year-old boys, contrasting them with the other age groups.

1.4.n: 袴着 is the name of a ceremony in which children first wear traditional hakama trousers.

2.0.n: 歳 counts years of age; の connects this age to 女子.

2.1.n: Links the age to 女子, describing the girls as seven years old.

2.2.n: Refers specifically to female children in this ceremony description.

2.3.n: Introduces the seven-year-old girls as the final age group.

2.4.n: 帯解 names the ceremony marking a switch from attached clothing ties to a proper obi sash.

2.5.n: Marks 帯解 as the ceremony that was performed.

2.6.n: Plain past form of 行う, used here for carrying out ceremonies.

2.7.n: Turns the preceding description of performing ceremonies into a noun-like phrase.

2.8.n: Marks the preceding fact as what constitutes the celebration’s origin in the next line.

3.0.n: First part of 七五三, the festival name referring to children aged seven, five, and three.

3.1.n: Middle part of the festival name 七五三, not a separate age statement here.

3.2.n: Final part of the festival name 七五三, which precedes 祝い.

3.3.n: Combines with 七五三 to refer to celebrating this children’s festival.

3.4.n: Links the celebration to its origin, 由来.

3.5.n: Identifies the earlier ceremonies as the historical basis of the celebration.

3.6.n: Politely ends the statement identifying the festival’s origin.

4.0.n: In これまで, これ points to the present time rather than a physical object.

4.1.n: Combines with これ to mean up to the present.

4.2.n: Lets これまで describe the children’s growth as growth up to now.

4.3.n: Japanese does not require this noun to specify singular or plural.

4.4.n: Links the children to their growth.

4.5.n: Refers to how the children have developed up to this point.

4.6.n: Marks what people are grateful for with 感謝する.

4.7.n: 感謝する becomes 感謝し to connect this action to the following actions without ending the sentence.

5.0.n: Points to the future, contrasting with これまで in the preceding line.

5.1.n: Links これから to the growth being wished for, placing it in the future.

5.2.n: Describes the children’s development and needs な before the noun 成長.

5.3.n: Connects 健やか to 成長 so it describes the kind of growth.

5.4.n: Refers here to the children’s future development.

5.5.n: Marks healthy future growth as what is wished for.

5.6.n: 願う becomes 願い to connect this wish to the invitation in the next line.

6.0.n: With の, describes the shrine as belonging to the surrounding community.

6.1.n: Links the local area to its shrine.

6.2.n: お宮 is a respectful term for a Shinto shrine, with お adding respect.

6.3.n: Marks the shrine as the destination of the worship visit.

6.4.n: Combines with みんな to include every family member.

6.5.n: After 家族, emphasizes that all family members take part.

6.6.n: Marks 家族みんな as the group doing the activity together.

6.7.n: お参りする becomes お参りしましょう, a polite invitation to visit a shrine or temple for worship.

0.lit: As for three-year-old boys and girls, the hair-growing ceremony;
0.tip: 髪 and 置 form one ceremony name, 髪置; the verb comes later.

1.lit: As for five-year-old boys, the first hakama-wearing ceremony;
1.tip: The repeated は contrasts the age groups and their respective ceremonies.

2.lit: As for seven-year-old girls, the fact that they performed the obi sash ceremony,
2.tip: 行ったことが gathers the preceding ceremony descriptions into the subject of the statement completed next.

3.lit: Is the origin of the Seven-Five-Three celebration.
3.tip: 七五三 is a single festival name, even though its three numbers are separate tap targets.

4.lit: Giving thanks for the children’s growth up to now,
4.tip: 感謝し connects to what follows; に marks what the gratitude is for.

5.lit: Wishing for healthy growth from now on,
5.tip: これから contrasts future growth with the growth so far expressed by これまで.

6.lit: To the local shrine, together as the whole family, let’s go to pray.
6.tip: しましょう politely invites the listener to join an action, like English let’s.
